    "start": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["next"]},
    "end": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": []},
    "command": {"runs": "worker", "next": ["next", "on_error"]},
    "condition": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["when", "else"]},
    "switch": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["cases", "default"]},
    "for_each": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["body", "next"], "bounded": True},
    "while": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["body", "next"], "bounded": True},
    "parallel": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["branches", "next"]},
    "delay": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["next"]},
    "approval": {"runs": "scheduler",
                 "next": ["on_approve", "on_reject", "on_timeout"]},
    "http": {"runs": "worker", "next": ["next", "on_error"]},
    "script": {"runs": "sandbox", "next": ["next", "on_error"]},
    "ai": {"runs": "ai", "next": ["next", "on_error"]},
    "transform": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["next"]},
    "set_var": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["next"]},
    "sub_playbook": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["next", "on_error"]},
    "incident_update": {"runs": "worker", "next": ["next"]},
    "task": {"runs": "scheduler", "next": ["next"]},
    "notification": {"runs": "worker", "next": ["next"]},
    # The abstract containment action. dispatch.py resolves it at run time
    # against whichever EDR has an agent on the host, so a playbook says
    # "isolate this" and never names a vendor. on_unsupported is a real
    # branch, not a courtesy: a containment that silently does nothing is
    # the worst outcome this platform can produce.
    "response": {"runs": "worker",
                 "next": ["next", "on_error", "on_unsupported"]},
}

props.doc:
The playbooks a client starts with.

One, deliberately: it is a worked example of every mechanism this platform
has that a generic automation tool does not - abstract containment that
resolves per EDR, an approval that cannot be bypassed by a timeout, an AI
step that is a command like any other, and an unsupported branch that makes
a containment nobody could perform visible instead of silent.

It is a starting point to edit, not a template to trust: the thresholds and
the auto-close are one SOC's judgement and every client argues with them.
props.name: shipped_playbooks

props.code:
triage = {
    "start": "begin",

    # Severity and auto-close live here, on the playbook, and not on the
    # intake form. Intake is about how an alert ARRIVES - the transport and
    # the shape of the vendor JSON. What the alert is worth and whether a
    # human ever sees it is a decision, it differs per client, it has to be
    # reviewable and versioned, and a decision that runs is a playbook step.
    "variables": [
        {"name": "severity_map", "type": "object", "scope": "execution",
         "initial": {"Critical": "critical", "High": "high",
                     "Medium": "medium", "Low": "low",
                     "Informational": "info"}},
        {"name": "close_rules", "type": "array", "scope": "execution",
         "initial": [{"field": "status", "value": "false_positive"},
                     {"field": "verdict", "value": "benign"}]},
    ],

    "nodes": {
        "begin": {"kind": "start", "name": "Alert arrives",
                  "next": "severity"},

        # The vendor says "High"; this client may or may not mean by that
        # what the next client means. The map is the edit an engineer makes
        # when onboarding, in a version they can point at later.
        "severity": {
            "kind": "command", "name": "Decide severity",
            "command": "alert.severity",
            "inputs": {"raw_severity": "{{ alert.raw.severity }}",
                       "severity_map": "{{ vars.severity_map }}",
                       "default_severity": "medium"},
            "output_var": "sev", "next": "autoclose", "on_error": "extract",
        },

        # Auto-close before enrichment, because the cheapest alert to handle
        # is the one nothing is spent on. The command returns WHICH rule
        # matched, so the closure is answerable.
        "autoclose": {
            "kind": "command", "name": "Should this close?",
            "command": "alert.should_close",
            "inputs": {"alert": "{{ alert }}",
                       "rules": "{{ vars.close_rules }}"},
            "output_var": "closing", "next": "closing?",
            "on_error": "extract",
        },

        "closing?": {
            "kind": "condition", "name": "Matched an auto-close rule?",
            "when": [{"if": "closing.close == true", "then": "closed"}],
            "else": "extract",
        },

        "closed": {
            "kind": "incident_update", "name": "Close it",
            "inputs": {"status": "closed",
                       "note": "Closed automatically: matched "
                               "{{ closing.matched }}."},
            "next": "done",
        },

        # Observables out of whatever the SIEM sent, refanged and
        # deduplicated, so every later step reads one shape.
        "extract": {
            "kind": "command", "name": "Extract observables",
            "command": "ioc.extract",
            "inputs": {"text": "{{ alert.description }}"},
            "next": "classify", "on_error": "handoff",
        },

        # The AI step is a command. It is given the alert and the
        # observables, and it must answer with one of the labels below -
        # a free-text answer that a branch has to parse is a decision
        # made by prose.
        "classify": {
            "kind": "ai", "name": "Classify the alert",
            "command": "ai.classify",
            "inputs": {
                "prompt": "Classify this alert for a SOC analyst.",
                "context": {"alert": "{{ alert }}",
                            "observables": "{{ steps.extract.indicators }}"},
                "labels": ["true_positive", "false_positive", "needs_review"],
            },
            "next": "decide", "on_error": "handoff",
        },

        "decide": {
            "kind": "condition", "name": "Confirmed malicious?",
            "when": [
                {"if": "steps.classify.label == 'true_positive'",
                 "then": "confident?"},
            ],
            "else": "review",
        },

        # Two clauses rather than one, because "it said malicious but it is
        # not sure" and "it said benign" are different situations and an
        # analyst reading the execution should be able to tell them apart.
        "confident?": {
            "kind": "condition", "name": "Confident enough to act?",
            "when": [
                {"if": "steps.classify.confidence >= 0.8",
                 "then": "approve_isolation"},
            ],
            "else": "review",
        },

        # Containment is HIGH risk, so a human decides. on_timeout goes to
        # the analyst queue rather than proceeding - an approval that
        # proceeds on a timeout is not an approval.
        "approve_isolation": {
            "kind": "approval", "name": "Approve host isolation",
            "action_key": "response.isolate_host",
            "summary": "Isolate {{ host.hostname }}",
            "risk_level": "high", "timeout_s": 1800,
            "on_approve": "isolate",
            "on_reject": "review",
            "on_timeout": "review",
        },

        # No vendor is named. The engine resolves this against whichever
        # EDR has an agent on THIS host, for THIS client.
        "isolate": {
            "kind": "response", "name": "Isolate the host",
            "action": "isolate_host",
            "inputs": {"target": "{{ host.hostname }}"},
            "next": "notify",
            "on_error": "handoff",
            "on_unsupported": "handoff",
        },

        "notify": {
            "kind": "notification", "name": "Tell the client",
            "inputs": {
                "to": "{{ inputs.notify_email }}",
                "subject": "Host isolated: {{ host.hostname }}",
                "body": "Contained automatically after analyst approval.",
            },
            "next": "contained",
        },

        "contained": {
            "kind": "incident_update", "name": "Mark contained",
            "inputs": {"status": "containment",
                       "note": "Host isolated; awaiting eradication."},
            "next": "done",
        },

        # Everything that is not a clean containment ends up in front of a
        # person, with the reason attached.
        "review": {
            "kind": "task", "name": "Analyst review",
            "inputs": {
                "title": "Review: {{ alert.title }}",
                "detail": "Classified {{ steps.classify.label }} at "
                          "{{ steps.classify.confidence }} confidence.",
                "assignee_role": "Analyst",
            },
            "next": "done",
        },

        "handoff": {
            "kind": "task", "name": "Automation could not finish",
            "inputs": {
                "title": "Manual containment: {{ alert.title }}",
                "detail": "A step failed or no connected EDR could act on "
                          "this host. The reason is on the execution.",
                "assignee_role": "Analyst",
            },
            "next": "done",
        },

        "done": {"kind": "end", "name": "End"},
    },
}

return [{
    "key": "edr.alert.triage",
    "name": "EDR alert triage and containment",
    "description": ("Extract observables, classify, ask a human before "
                    "containing, then isolate through whichever EDR can "
                    "reach the host."),
    "category": "triage",
    "technique_ids": ["T1078", "T1059"],
    "definition": triage,
}]

props.doc:
Give a client the shipped playbooks, as drafts.

Drafts, never published. Publishing is a decision about a specific
customer's estate and risk appetite, and a platform that published on the
client's behalf would be automating containment nobody agreed to.
props.name: install_shipped_playbooks

props.code:
from soar.platform.ids import new_id

import hashlib
import json

installed = 0
for shipped in shipped_playbooks():
    problems = validate_playbook(shipped["definition"])
    if problems:
        raise RuntimeError("shipped playbook %s is invalid: %s"
                           % (shipped["key"], "; ".join(problems)))

    existing = db.query(
        "SELECT id FROM playbook WHERE org_id = %s AND key = %s",
        [org_id, shipped["key"]], org_id)
    if existing:
        continue

    playbook_id = new_id("pb")
    db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO playbook (id, org_id, key, name, description, "
        "category, technique_ids, owner_id) "
        "VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s)",
        [playbook_id, org_id, shipped["key"], shipped["name"],
         shipped["description"], shipped["category"],
         shipped["technique_ids"], "platform"],
        org_id)

    # Hashed over the definition, so two versions carrying the same graph
    # are recognisably the same graph.
    body = json.dumps(shipped["definition"], sort_keys=True,
                      separators=(",", ":"))
    version_id = new_id("pbv")
    db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO playbook_version (id, playbook_id, version, state, "
        "definition, content_sha256, created_by) "
        "VALUES (%s,%s,1,'draft',%s,%s,%s)",
        [version_id, playbook_id, body,
         hashlib.sha256(body.encode("utf-8")).digest(), "platform"],
        org_id)
    db.execute(
        "UPDATE playbook SET current_version_id = %s WHERE id = %s",
        [version_id, playbook_id], org_id)
    installed += 1
return installed
